headline: Uttarakhand: 12-year-old boy mauled to death, 3rd child killed in leopard attack in 6 days - The Times of India
summary: A 12-year-old boy was mauled to death, marking the third child killed in leopard attacks in six days.
article_body:
DEHRADUN: In the past six days, three children have lost their lives to leopard attacks in Uttarakhand. The latest attack was on Sunday, when a 12-year-old boy was mauled to death by a leopard in Tehri. 
On November 24, a nine-year-old boy died in a leopard attack in Almora district. On November 22, a five-year-old child was similarly killed in Pauri Garhwal.
Till date this year, 50 deaths have been reported in man-animal conflicts as per data collated by the forest department. 
Every year, the maximum number of wildlife attacks, an estimated 70% (around 35 deaths, according to a source in the forest department), have been due to leopard attacks.
Each death is a chilling reminder of the vulnerability of people living in villages close to jungles. In Sunday's incident, which took place at Maykot village, 12-year-old Arnav Chand had gone out to play with his friends but did not return home in the evening. When his panicked parents and a frontline forest team started a search, they found the boy's mutilated corpse in the forest.
Villagers are now worried the leopard is on the prowl and will hunt on other children or elderly or disabled persons. The forest department has placed camera traps and cages and deployed additional force. 
"Permission from the chief wildlife warden has been sought to trap the leopard," said VK Singh, divisional forest officer (DFO), Tehri.On November 25, nine-year-old Aarav Singh, a class-3 student, was killed when a leopard lurking in the courtyard of his house pounced on him and dragged him to a nearby forest. Similarly, on November 22 evening, five-year-old Piyush was killed by a leopard while playing with his friends. Villagers tried to come to the rescue of the child but it was too late. The forest department claimed it had trapped the leopard two days after the incident. Experts monitoring these incidents say that women and children are the most vulnerable since they are the ones who mostly fall victims to leopard attacks. According to the latest estimate by Doon-based Wildlife Institute of India, Uttarakhand is home to 800-1,200 leopards.
In the hill state, winters see heightened leopard attacks. Scientifically, neither the forest department nor wildlife experts have established the specific reason behind this. However, common reasons behind such attacks are said to be leopards' mating season, which is in winter, lack of lights in and around houses in the chilly season and waste strewn around.Last week, the Uttarakhand high court had heard a PIL on increased leopard attacks in the state and asked the government to form an expert committee to address the issue urgently.

headline: Leopard mauls 4 year old girl to death in Pauri Village - Garhwal Post
summary: 4-year-old girl mauled to death by leopard in Pauri Village, Uttarakhand.
article_body:
Garhwal Post Bureau
Pauri Garhwal, 3 Apr: Leopard attacks persist unabated in Pauri Garhwal district, casting a pall of fear and insecurity over rural pockets. In yet another gut-wrenching episode late last night, a four-year-old girl fell victim to a leopard in Bhatkot village under Chaubattakhal tehsil’s Kunjkhali area in Gaadri gram sabha. The child, Drishti, daughter of Harendra Singh, was playing in the courtyard after dinner at around 9 p.m. when the lurking predator pounced, clamped her in its jaws and dragged her towards the fields below. Family members raised frantic cries, drawing other villagers who joined the desperate search through the night.
Some locals claimed that the girl was sitting with her father Harendra Singh, mother Savita Devi and her elder sister Deepanshi in the kitchen around 9 p.m. when the leopard attacked her and dragged her to the forest while some others claimed that Drishti was playing in her courtyard when the leopard attacked her. The leopard seized the girl suddenly and bolted towards the jungle. Despite exhaustive efforts, her mutilated body was found about two-and-a-half kilometres away in a stream after an intensive search by the villagers, sending waves of grief through the village. The incident site was promptly notified to forest and revenue officials. The locals are outraged over the recurring strikes by the predator.
It may also be recalled that earlier on 21 March, a leopard had attacked and injured an elderly man in Khirsu. The villagers lament that leopards now roam brazenly near homes, singling out children and rendering village life perilous. Anguish mounts against the forest department, with incessant demands for decisive intervention. The Bhatkot residents have demanded that the leopard be proclaimed a man-eater and eliminated swiftly to avert future horrors and safeguard lives. The villagers have lambasted the administration, highlighting the leopard’s prolonged rampage targeting children and women without tangible action.
Meanwhile, DFO Pauri Mahatim Yadav claimed that the forest teams arrived at the scene immediately after the alert. Patrols stand reinforced across the area, with traps deployed and a specialised squad constituted to nab the beast. He has urged the local villagers to stay calm near the site, warning that the leopard could return to its prey. The episode has once again starkly exposed the intensifying human-wildlife conflict in Uttarakhand’s mountainous hamlets, where such clashes have turned everyday existence into a nightmare.

The Forest department was immediately informed and its team arrived at the site to begin investigation and launch a search for the leopard. Local MLA Dilip Rawat was also apprised of the incident. They said that rising wildlife activity has made it increasingly risky to enter forests and fields, instilling constant fear among residents.
At the same time, Pauri Forest Division SDO Ayesha Bisht stated that the department has deployed cages and trap cameras to monitor the leopard’s movements. A trained shooter has also been stationed in the area to take swift action if required. She assured that every possible effort is being made to provide relief to villagers and appealed to residents not to venture alone into forests or deserted areas. She urged that any sighting of the leopard should be immediately reported to the Forest department.
It may be recalled that in the hills of Uttarakhand and particularly in Pauri districts, leopard attacks on humans have become very frequent with many people losing their life. Garhwal Post Bureau

They state that leopard activity has been escalating in the area for a long time and despite several complaints, the forest department has failed to take decisive action. They asserted that had timely measures been adopted, the tragedy could have been averted.
The rising frequency of such incidents has left locals living in fear in many villages across the district particularly where the leopard and the bear attacks have been reported. The leopard attacks and the sightings have made it difficult for them to step out of their homes after dusk. The villagers have warned that they will be compelled to launch a mass agitation if concrete steps are not taken without delay.

The sudden and ferocious attack proved fatal, with Rajendra succumbing to his injuries instantly. News of the incident spread rapidly, plunging the village into grief and panic. His family was shattered, the community was overwhelmed with sorrow, and fear engulfed the entire region.
Following the incident, the villagers expressed their outrage at the Forest Department, accusing the officials of negligence in addressing the growing menace. Women and children, they said, are too frightened to leave their homes, and even venturing into isolated areas during the day has become perilous.

headline: Uttarakhand forest officials try to capture tiger that killed 2 in December - Down To Earth
summary: A tiger killed two people in December.
article_body:
After the mauled body of a person was found in the Corbett-Ramnagar forest area on December 25, 2022, joint forest teams have started investigating the area and setting up camera traps to find the tiger.
The man, identified as Abdul Rashid, was drinking with two friends in an area of the jungle where movement is restricted after sunrise and sunset.
“It is unfortunate that such a thing has happened. The forest department takes out regular convoys on the highways to ask people not to wander out into the forest after dark as it can prove to be risky,“ said Samir Sinha, chief wildlife warden, Uttarakhand. “We are now trying to capture the tiger.”
Two teams have been deployed to tranquilise the tiger, he told Down To Earth.
The tiger is also suspected to have killed another man on December 12. Camera traps and cages have been set up in the forest to trace the movement of the tiger and capture it as soon as possible.
“We are trying to capture the tiger and are requesting the people for their cooperation and stay indoors after sunset. We have requested them to not venture outside unless absolutely necessary,” Sinha shared.
However, the department has no plans to put the tiger down. “We are following the protocol that states we need to try and capture the animal alive as far as possible,” said Sinha, adding:
In case a tough decision needs to be taken, we will do so in due time, following the proper procedure. So far, our aim is to capture the animal alive.
The officials have also not decided whether they will release the tiger in another forest to avoid more conflict with humans in the future after it is captured or if they will send it to a zoo, according to Sinha.
“It is premature to say where the tiger will be sent after being captured. We will keep it in the cage for a few days and observe it and verify certain parameters before making this decision,” he said.
According to the newspaper The Times of India, there are around 230 tigers in the stretch between Aamdanda checkpost in Corbett and Mohand checkpost in Almora. There have been 13 deaths due to tiger attacks in the state in 2022, the highest in 22 years.

headline: Record 43 deaths from tiger and leopard attacks in Uttarakhand this year - The New Indian Express
summary: A total of 43 deaths have been recorded from tiger and leopard attacks in Uttarakhand this year.
article_body:
DEHRADUN: In the 23 years since its formation, Uttarakhand has seen a record high of 43 fatalities in human-wildlife conflicts involving tigers and leopards this year. Of these, 21 individuals fell victim to leopard attacks, while 22 lost their lives in tiger encounters.
According to data gathered by the forest department, between January 2000 and December 2023, a total of 551 people lost their lives in leopard and tiger attacks, with over 1,833 individuals sustaining injuries. Additionally, since June 2001, a total of 1,663 leopard deaths have been recorded, with many attributed to accidents or inter-species conflicts, among other causes.
According to 2023 data from the state forest department, the population of leopards and tigers in Uttarakhand has seen an increase since 2015. The estimated number of leopards in Uttarakhand is 3,115, while in 2015 the number was 2,335. These figures are significant as Uttarakhand is one of the states where human-leopard conflicts are frequently.
While there are now 12,852 leopards in India, the previous estimate made in 2014 was 7,910. The population has registered an increase of more than 60 percent.
Speaking to The New Indian Express, Chief Wildlife Warden Sameer Sinha voiced his apprehension regarding the increasing occurrences of conflict. "The estimates of the leopard population will provide us with valuable insights into the problem areas, and we are committed to taking measures to alleviate the situation," said Sinha.
A spokesman of the forest department told TNIE, "In the year 2023, 21 people died in leopard attacks and 22 people died in tiger attacks in the incidents of human-wildlife conflict in the state, which is 13 per cent more than the previous year." Incidents of elephant attacks have decreased this year, with five people losing their lives compared to 12 last year.
The Wildlife Protection Society of India (WPSI), a wildlife conservation organisation that monitors tiger and leopard mortality, has released data showing 204 deaths in the country this year during the period from January 1 to December 26. The 43 deaths of tigers and leopards in Uttarakhand represent 15 per cent of the country's total.
According to official sources in the Uttarakhand forest department, the state has officially recorded the third-largest tiger population in the country, with a total of 560. The Corbett Tiger Reserve (CTR) has reported the highest number of tigers at 260 among the 53 tiger reserves in the nation. Notably, the tiger population in Uttarakhand has surged from 442 to 560 compared to the figures reported in 2018.

According to residents, around a dozen incidents have reportedly taken place in the area, raising serious concerns about the safety of people, particularly those living in or around forested and isolated stretches.
The repeated presence of the wild animal has created a sense of insecurity among villagers, with many residents reportedly avoiding unnecessary movement during vulnerable hours. The situation has also become a matter of concern for families, farmers and others who are required to travel through the area during the early morning and evening.
Following the reports, a team from the Wildlife Department has reached the spot and is closely monitoring the situation. Officials are keeping a watch on the movement of the leopard and assessing the circumstances in which the animal has been entering areas inhabited or frequented by local residents.
The Wildlife Department is also expected to take necessary measures to prevent further incidents and ensure the safety of both the local population and the wild animal. Residents have been urged to cooperate with the department and immediately report any fresh sighting or unusual movement of the leopard to the concerned authorities.
Meanwhile, locals have been advised to remain particularly cautious and avoid moving alone, especially during the early morning and evening hours when the risk of encountering wildlife may be higher. People have also been urged not to approach, chase or attempt to confront the animal if spotted.
The repeated incidents have intensified calls from residents for effective preventive measures and increased patrolling in vulnerable areas. Villagers are seeking timely intervention from the concerned authorities to restore a sense of security and prevent any further attacks or untoward incidents.

Leopard Kills 10-Yr-Old In UP's Balrampur, Villagers Asked To Stay On Alert
A 10-year-old boy was killed by a leopard in Uttar Pradesh's Balrampur district. Police and forest forces have increased patrolling in the region and advised villagers to stay vigilant.
A leopard killed a 10-year-old boy in Uttar Pradesh's Balrampur district when he had gone to graze goats in a forest area. Police officials told news agency IANS that villagers of Dharampur village rushed to save Sameer Ansari when they heard his shrieks, however, they were not able to make it on time and the boy died.
Station Head Officer (SHO), Hariya, Govind Kumar told IANS, “Hearing the boy’s shrieks, many villagers rushed to the spot with sticks and began making a noise to scare away the big cat. However, by the time the villagers could reach the spot, the leopard had already severed the head of the boy. Later the family members arrived and took him to hospital.”
The victim's father Shafiq Ansari was in Mumbai when his wife told him that their son had been missing since Tuesday afternoon.
The forest department has deployed teams in order to catch the leopard and a team of police and forest officials are patrolling the area, IANS reported.
Forest Range Officer KP Singh said that the villagers have been advised to remain alert so that they could try to protect themselves better from leopards.
DFO Balrampur, Semmaran, told IANS that the forces will take assistance from infra-red drones to catch the big cat. The DFO added that the forest department is also taking other steps to ensure protection to the villagers by increasing patrolling and installing camera traps to monitor any leopard activity.
Recently, two leopards were trapped using IR drones in Bahraich, as reported by IANS.
Earlier in September, a four-year-old girl was mauled to death by a leopard in Jammu & Kashmir’s Udhampur district. Locals discovered the body about 2 kilometres in Upper Bhanjala village of Panchari tehsil in the district, as reported by news agency ANI. The deceased was identified as Tanu.

headline: Human-wildlife conflict: 2 killed, over 40 injured in bear attacks across Kashmir since apple harvest began - Greater Kashmir
summary: Bear attacks have resulted in casualties across Kashmir.
article_body:
More than 40 people have been injured and two killed in bear attacks across Kashmir since apple harvesting began in August, with animals increasingly straying into orchards, maize fields and nearby settlements.
South Kashmir has recorded 12 injuries and one death in the Anantnag-Kulgam wildlife range, while the Pulwama-Shopian range has reported eight injuries so far, taking the total in the region to 20.
Central Kashmir has recorded eight injuries, and north Kashmir has recorded 16 injuries and one death.
In Kulgam, 45-year-old Latifa Banoo was mauled to death on Aug. 31 while working in an orchard at Tarigam village.
Her family learned of the attack only after she was shifted to SDH Qaimoh by the villagers.
“We are devastated by her death. Authorities should step in to prevent such incidents and ensure that no more lives are lost,” her family said.
Days earlier, 68-year-old Abdul Salam Teeli of Ahmadabad village in the D.H. Pora area of the same district was seriously injured after going to the aid of another orchard worker, Bilal Ahmad Kohli, who had cried for help.
“When I heard the cries, I rushed to help him, along with my wife and daughter-in-law. I saw Kohli lying injured. The bear then turned towards me and attacked me as well,” Teeli said.
“Such a time should never come again in my life. The moment was like a heart attack.”
This spike in attacks has been reported across Kashmir
In the latest attacks, Mohammad Maqbool Bhat was seriously injured at Mirmadan in Dooru, Anantnag, on Sep 3, while another man was injured at Lalwani Seer village of the same district today, on Sep 6.
He was immediately shifted to GMC Anantnag, from where he has been referred to SKIMS, Srinagar.
Wildlife Warden Anantnag-Kulgam Sajad Bhat said August and September are particularly sensitive because ripening apples and maize draw bears into areas where people are working.
In Pulwama, Ghulam Nabi Bhat, 55, a flour-mill worker from Jawbehara, Awantipora was also grievously injured, at his workplace.
Six more people were also injured in separate bear attacks in the Tral area.
In Shopian, a minor girl was injured in a leopard attack in Dragad village on August 4.
Earlier, towards the end of July, three people, including a woman were injured in a bear attack in Reshipora-Harmain in the same district.
Central Kashmir saw three people mauled at Khonmoh, Srinagar, within 24 hours on Aug 16 and 17.
In Budgam’s Rawatpora-Khag, a man, Abdul Qayoom Thokar was critically injured in a bear attack, while in Ganderbal Mohammad Maqbool Bhat was attacked by the animal at Watalbagh , leaving him grievously injured.
In north Kashmir’s Kupwara district, 6-year-old Subahat Jan was killed in a bear attack at Nichama village.
In Bandipora, Javid Ahmad Pir was mauled at Kralgund-Hajin, while Farooq Ahmad Khan suffered severe facial injuries at Chrawan in Ajas.
In Baramula, a man Firdous Ahmad Mir and a woman Zahida Begum were injured while cutting grass at Janwara in Sopore.
“Last year, also during the apple harvest season, we lived in constant fear of wildlife attacks, and this year is no different,” said orchardist Mohammad Sultan of Kupwara.
Wildlife Warden North Kashmir Suhail Intesar said August and September are the peak months for bear encounters.
“Once apples ripen, bears come down to orchards. This has become an annual phenomenon,” Intesar said.
Leopard sightings have also increased, with animals turning up closer to villages and homes. A child was injured in a leopard attack in Shopian.
Wildlife Warden Pulwama-Shopian Suhail Wagay warned against leaving children alone in areas where leopards have been sighted.
“Children are mostly their prey, so they should not be left alone, particularly in areas where leopards have been sighted,” Wagay said.
Wildlife teams have tranquilised and captured many animals, while others were driven away before they could cause harm. In Pulwama and Shopian alone, 46 animals have been removed from human habitations since the harvest began - 22 black bears, 21 leopards and three others.
“These animals were actually present in human habitations. We responded immediately, rescued them and did not allow them to cause any damage due to the quick response,” Wagay said.
Control rooms have been activated across wildlife divisions. Orchard workers and residents have been advised to move in groups, avoid fields during evening and after-dark hours, carry torches and report sightings immediately.
With the harvest continuing through November, officials have urged people living and working near forest fringes to remain vigilant.

headline: Leopard kills one, injures five in multiple attacks across Himachal’s Mandi district - The New Indian Express

article_body:
CHANDIGARH: One person was killed and five others injured after a leopard carried out a series of attacks at three different locations in the Balh Ghati area of Himachal Pradesh’s Mandi district on Tuesday morning before being shot dead by locals, officials said.
The leopard attacked people in Chandiyal, Bhadyal and Malwana villages, triggering panic among residents. According to officials, the animal first struck at Chandiyal, after which it moved to Bhadyal, injuring several people, and finally reached Malwana village, where it mauled a 40-year-old man, Balveer Singh, resulting in his death.
Singh, a resident of Bholi village, was a migrant worker living in Mandi and had come to Malwana to visit relatives. All those attacked sustained paw-related injuries and were immediately shifted to hospital, where doctors described their condition as stable.
Sources said forest department teams were rushed to the affected villages soon after the first alerts were received. As panic and chaos gripped the area, villagers reportedly came out of their homes armed with sticks and sharp implements in an attempt to protect themselves.
The leopard was eventually killed when it tried to attack again. Its carcass has been taken into custody and sent for post-mortem examination.
The injured have been identified as Sahib Singh, a native of Bihar; Dinanath of Bhadyal; Rekha Devi, wife of Dinanath; Janit, also from Bhadyal; and Champa Devi of Malwana. They have been admitted to Shri Lal Bahadur Shastri Government Medical College and Hospital, Nerchowk, where they are undergoing treatment.
Confirming the leopard attack, an official of the local administration said one person had died, five others were injured and the animal had also been killed.
Following the incident, forest officials have intensified surveillance in and around the affected villages. Locals have been advised to avoid venturing out alone during early morning and late evening hours, when wildlife movement is more likely.
An inquiry is underway to determine how and why the leopard entered densely populated areas, once again highlighting the growing human–wildlife conflict in the region.

headline: Seven killed in 20 days as tiger attacks spike in Uttarakhand - The New Indian Express
summary: There has been a spike in tiger attacks leading to seven deaths in Uttarakhand.
article_body:
DEHRADUN: The escalating crisis of human wildlife conflict in Uttarakhand has taken a grim turn, with a sharp spike in fatal tiger attacks eclipsing earlier concerns over bear encounters.
The state has recorded seven human deaths due to wildlife encounters in January alone, four of which are directly attributed to tigers.
The surge signals a worrying trend following a year marked by heavy losses. In 2025, the state reported 68 deaths from human wildlife interactions, with an alarming 488 people sustaining injuries, along with extensive losses to livestock and crops.
While bear attacks had dominated concern over the past six months, officials are now grappling with increased aggression from big cats.
According to sources in the Forest Department, the anticipated decline in bear attacks owing to lower temperatures and hibernation has not fully materialised, but attention has now shifted decisively to tigers.
In just the first 20 days of this month, four people were killed in tiger attacks across sensitive areas, including the Kalagarh Tiger Reserve, Ramnagar and the Terai East Forest Division. Leopard attacks have claimed two more lives a woman in the Nainital Forest Division and another person in Bada Gaon in Pauri.
A comparison with last year underlines the gravity of the current situation. In 2023, tiger attacks resulted in 12 deaths and five injuries. Leopard attacks were even deadlier, causing 19 deaths and injuring 102 people over the year.
Principal Chief Conservator of Forests (PCCF) Ranjan Mishra acknowledged the heightened risk and issued an urgent advisory to residents living along forest fringes.
“This period coincides with the tiger’s breeding season, making them potentially more territorial and aggressive,” Mishra said. “We strongly advise residents to avoid entering forests unless absolutely necessary.”
He outlined basic precautions for essential travel: “If you must venture out, ensure you move in groups, make noise to alert wildlife to your presence, and take every possible safety measure.”
The Forest Department said intensified awareness drives and protective measures are being rolled out across vulnerable districts to prevent further loss of life.

Efforts to Capture the Leopard

headline: Woman mauled to death in tiger attack in Champawat - The Times of India

The tiger attacked Virma Devi from behind and dragged her deep into the forest. A search operation was launched by a forest department team after the women accompanying Devi rushed back to inform villagers. Devi's mutilated body was found in the bushes three hours later, about 500m from where she was attacked. After a post-mortem exam at Tanakpur hospital in Champawat, her body was handed over to her family, said Surendra Singh Koranga, SHO of Banbasa police station. 
Khatima sub-divisional forest officer Sachita Verma said evidence from the site confirmed a tiger attack. She added that necessary measures were being taken to ensure public safety. 
Residents in the area said they were afraid to step out of their homes, especially in the evenings, as this is the second tiger-related death in the region in two months. In Feb, a 35-year-old man was killed while grazing cattle near Tukdi village in Nanakmatta area of Udham Singh Nagar district. "We demand immediate action to capture the tiger before another tragedy occurs," said Deepak Chandra Rajwar, head administrator of Devipura. The forest department has intensified patrolling in the area and plans to install a cage to trap the tiger. 
Since its formation in 2000, Uttarakhand has recorded a high number of fatalities due to tiger attacks. From Jan 2000 to Dec 2023, 551 people were killed and over 1,833 injured in leopard and tiger attacks combined. 
The number of tiger-related deaths has fluctuated in recent years. In 2022, 11 people were killed, which doubled to 22 in 2023. Seven such deaths were reported in 2024. With Uttarakhand's tiger population increasing from 442 in 2018 to 560, human-wildlife conflict has risen, driving the need for urgent and effective strategies to ensure the safety of both humans and wildlife.

headline: 2 injured in separate bear attacks in Tral - Greater Kashmir
summary: Two people injured in separate bear attacks.
article_body:
Pulwama, Sep 3: Two people, including a woman, were injured in separate bear attacks in Tral areas of South Kashmir's Pulwama district on Thursday. In view of the increasing frequency of such attacks, the Wildlife Department plans to use radio/GPS collars to track animals trapped in populated areas and released back into their natural habitats.
Ghulam Nabi Bhat, son of Abdul Rahim Bhat and a resident of Syed Abad Pastuna, was injured when a bear attacked him in Pastuna village. In a separate incident at Tral Bala, a woman identified as Shareef Begum, wife of Riyaz Ahmad Bhat, was also injured in a bear attack.
Shareef Begum was initially taken to Sub-District Hospital Tral and was later shifted to SMHS Hospital Srinagar for further treatment, according to news agency KNT.
The incidents have brought renewed attention to a question that has remained difficult to answer in Kashmir's recurring human-bear encounters: what happens after a bear is trapped and released away from a populated area?
Wildlife Range Officer Khangund, Tral Range, Muhammad Younis told the news agency that the department has trapped dozens of bears from different areas and released them in their habitats. He said the proposed use of collar-based tracking would help determine whether animals released after capture subsequently return towards residential areas.
"Our team traps the wild animals wherever they appear," Younis said, adding that tracking the animals after release would provide a clearer picture of their movement and behaviour.
The proposed approach is not without precedent. Kashmir has already been part of radio-collaring research involving bears. A Wildlife SOS and J&K Wildlife Protection Department project launched in 2023 fitted six Himalayan brown bears with GPS-enabled radio collars to study their movements, habitat use and interaction with human settlements.
Earlier Wildlife Institute of India research in the Dachigam landscape also used radio-collaring to study Asiatic black bears, including their movement and use of different habitats. Such tracking can show whether a captured animal remains within its release habitat, moves towards human settlements or repeatedly follows particular routes.
The significance of such monitoring is growing as bear encounters continue to occur around villages, orchards and other areas of human activity in Kashmir. A recent study of human-black bear conflict in South Kashmir has linked the problem to factors including habitat degradation and reduced natural resources, while researchers have also examined how bears use landscapes containing both forest and human habitation.
J&K recorded 15,661 human-wildlife conflict incidents over two years, with 32 deaths and 350 injuries, according to figures presented by the government in February 2026. The figures underline the scale of the challenge facing communities as well as wildlife managers.
For Tral, Thursday's two attacks again bring the issue into sharp focus. If collar-based monitoring is introduced, the resulting movement data could help establish whether repeated appearances of bears in residential areas are linked to the same animals being relocated, their habitual movement routes, availability of food near settlements, or broader changes in habitat use.

headline: Fear grips Mussoorie residents as leopard attacks hotel worker on street - The Times of India
summary: Leopard attacked a hotel worker on the street in Mussoorie.
article_body:
MUSSOORIE: Fear has gripped the residents of Mussoorie after a 34-year-old man was attacked by a leopard on the busy Gandhi Chowk. Monu Thakur, who works at a local hotel, was returning home after work when the big cat pounced on him on Wednesday night. Thakur told TOI that he fought off the animal with his bare hands and is glad that he lived to tell the tale.
âI had seen the leopard near my employerâs residence in Gandhi Chowk earlier in the evening. We had used crackers and sticks to scare it away. But the leopard sprang up on me later that night when I was walking past that route. If it wasnât for my jacket, the animalâs claws would have dug deep into my skin. I held the front paws of the animal to save myself. At the same time, I took the support of the railing I was leaning on and pushed the leopard. It fell back and I ran for my life.â
 Captain Kamaljit Singh, the owner of the hotel and near whose residence the attack took place, said that he had sighted a leopard cub in the evening. âIâve seen leopards in forests but to see it on a busy location like Library Chowk was surprising,â he said. Residents said that this was the fifth leopard sighting since the last week of October. A female leopard was spotted on the Woodstock School road in October and days later, a giant leopard was caught on three CCTV cameras on Camelâs Back Road. There were two more sightings on Spring Road.
 Meanwhile, officials from the forest department have instructed people not to step out alone at night and have also promised increased vigil. âThis was a rare incident. The cub had lost its way from the jungle and come to the town. The mother came looking for the cub and was aggressive for the same reason,â said forest officer Hoshiyar Singh Pundir.
 Local residents said that the sightings seem to have increased over the years. Khushpal Singh Chandok, a local resident said, âMany of us have seen leopards in quieter parts of the hill town in peak winter. This time of the year is a little too early for them to be around.â

headline: Fourth human kill by Corbett tiger in 2 months - The Times of India
summary: The fourth human killed by a tiger in Corbett in two months.
article_body:
NAINITAL: A 32-year-old woman of Patrani Kargil village near Nainital was mauled to death by a tiger in Corbett Tiger Reserve (CTR) on Wednesday, marking the fourth human fatality since October 18 in the reserve. Earlier, three workers in the reserve were killed by prowling cats in Bijrani and Paterpani areas in November and October respectively.
This year, Uttarakhand has had at least 9 human lives lost to tiger attacks, with four occurring in CTR alone. While four people were left brutally injured in the attacks in Corbett, nine tigers have also died this year in the reserve owing to multiple reasons ranging from agerelated ailments to territorial fights. âIn the past six months, our staff has con- ducted workshops sensitising around 2000 people in and around Corbett about the increasing tiger population. Despite this, villagers often neglect the importance of taking precautions.
In the recent incident, the woman had ventured almost a kilometer inside the forests to collect wood,â said Dheeraj Pandey, director of CTR. He added that âa drone team and camera traps have been deployed to identify the tiger.â
According to officials, the victim of the recent attack, Anita Devi (32) had gone into the forest with two other wo- men to collect wood when a prowling tiger attacked Anita. Frightened, the other two women ran away and informed forest officials about the entire episode. After combing the area, they found Anitaâs body around 1 km inside the forest.
According to wildlife conservationists, the rising cases of human-wildlife conflict are mainly due to rising wildlife population, fragmentation of habitat, encroached wildlife corridors and urbanisation of fringe forests area.

headline: Rudraprayag: Leopard mauls elderly man to death - The Times of India

DEHRADUN: A 50-year-old man was mauled to death by a leopard in Jakholi area of Rudraprayag district on Wednesday. The victim was going to collect fodder for animals when the leopard attacked him at around 12 noon. 
The victim, Madan Singh Bisht (50) was a resident of Satni village in Rudraprayagâs Jakhola block. His body was discovered by his family members after a long search.
Sources said that the villagers started a protest against the forest department officials as they didnât reach the spot even after several hours of killing. However, Mahipal Singh Sirohi, Assistant Conservator of Forest (ACF), Rudraprayag, denied the allegation saying that a forest ranger reached the spot soon after getting information of the killing.

We have completed the formalities and the body was handed over to the family,â said Sirohi who claimed that Rudraprayag has witnessed an incident of leopard attack after five years. âIn the three years of my posting here, I never heard of a leopard attack. This is the first such attack in this region in years. However, it cannot be denied that the number of big cats is rising in Uttarakhand and we must find out ways to ensure that man-animal conflict incidents do not take place,â said the official.
Notably, this is the fourth case of leopard attack in Uttarakhand in just over a monthâs time. Earlier on October 2, a 10-year-old girl Meenakshi was killed in a leopard attack in Kulmori village of Pabo block. In another case, a 62-year-old man was killed by a leopard in Udal village of Bhaisiachhana block in Almora on October 8. headline: Himachal youth survives leopard attack after daring 12-minute struggle in Solan village - The Tribune
summary: A youth survived a leopard attack after a 12-minute struggle.
article_body:
Himachal youth survives leopard attack after daring 12-minute struggle in Solan village
ITI student overpowers animal that attacked him in fields near Arki; suffers minor injuries
Leopards are rarely killed by humans and such incidents usually occur during man-animal conflict when the big cats are attacked in retaliation for targeting livestock or humans. In a rare incident, a youth in Sarli village of Arki subdivision in Solan district fought off a leopard that attacked him and killed the animal after a prolonged struggle on Monday morning.
The incident occurred around 7 am when Pravesh Sharma was crossing his fields to fetch milk. A leopard, which was lurking in the fields, suddenly attacked him.
Despite the sudden assault, Pravesh did not lose his presence of mind and grappled with the animal for nearly 10 to 12 minutes. During the fierce struggle, he managed to grab the leopard by its jaws and eventually overpowered the animal, killing it by smashing its neck. The leopard was reportedly a year-old female.
Pravesh, a student of the Industrial Training Institute (ITI) in Arki, sustained multiple scratches on his body during the struggle but did not suffer any serious injuries.
His uncle, Shyam Lal, said leopard movement had been reported in the area earlier on March 6 and villagers had informed the Forest Department about it. Residents had also requested the authorities to install a cage to capture the animal. Locals further claimed that the leopard had attempted to attack a scooter rider around 7.30 am on Monday, forcing him to abandon his vehicle and flee.
Forest Divisional Officer Rajkumar Sharma visited the spot and provided immediate relief of Rs 5,000 to the injured youth. Rajkumar said increasing human intrusion and shrinking natural habitats were forcing wild animals to stray into human settlements.
“Leopards generally attack people and livestock at night. This incident occurred early in the morning, reflecting the desperation of the young animal,” he said. He added that forest officials were working to create awareness among villagers so that wild animals could be safely driven back into forest areas. Capturing a leopard by installing cages, he said, is a technically complex task that requires trained experts.
As news of Pravesh’s bravery spread in the area, residents praised the youth for his courage. Teachers and students of his alma mater, ITI Arki, also enquired about his wellbeing after learning about the incident.

headline: Himachal: Leopard kills 16 sheep in Chamba village, six missing - The Tribune

headline: Leopard kills youth in Mandi, injures eight - The Tribune
summary: Leopard killed a youth and injured eight others in Mandi.
article_body:
Panic gripped the Balh valley in Mandi district on Wednesday morning after a leopard attacked residents of three villages, killing one person and injuring eight others.
The reign of terror ended when alert villagers united and killed the leopard. The leopard first attacked residents in Chandyal village during the early hours, creating chaos and fear. It then moved to Bhadyal village, where it again attacked people indiscriminately. Four persons sustained serious injuries in these two villages. The leopard later reached Malwana village, where it fatally attacked a youth.
According to eyewitnesses, the youth was reportedly living in Mandi city and had come to the Balh valley to visit relatives. The deceased, identified as Balbir Singh, a native of Bheuli, died on the spot.
The injured include Sahib Singh, Deenanath, Champa Devi, Janit and Rekha Devi. The injured were rushed to Shri Lal Bahadur Shastri Medical College, Nerchowk, where they are undergoing treatment.
Following the attack, panic spread across the Balh valley. Residents came out of their homes carrying sticks and other improvised weapons to protect themselves. When the leopard attempted another attack, the villagers killed the animal. The leopard’s body has been sent for a post-mortem examination.
Teams from the administration, police and the Forest Department rushed to the spot to take stock of the situation.
Balh SDM Smritika Negi confirmed the incident and said immediate relief was being provided to the deceased’s family, while all possible assistance was being extended to the injured. All victims are out of danger. After an autopsy, the body of the deceased was handed over to his relatives for the last rites.
Mandi Divisional Forest Officer Vasu Doegar said a forest team immediately visited the spot and found the male leopard dead. It seemed the animal lost its territory and entered human habitation, he said.

headline: Two injured in bear attacks in Himachal in Chamba, Solan - The Times of India

article_body:
Shimla: Two people were injured in separate bear attacks in Chamba and Solan districts of Himachal Pradesh on Tuesday. While a youth was injured seriously after he came face to face with a bear in Deola panchayat in Chamba district, a woman received severe injured when she was attacked by a bear in a forested area of Devthal, Solan district, in the morning.
In Chamba, Deola village native Chaman Lal was returning home in the evening when a bear came in front of him.
Before Chaman could realize the lurking danger, the bear pounced on him and mauled his head, face and other body parts.
On hearing Chaman cry for help, passersby rushed towards him. Seeing the people approaching him, the bear fled. Chaman was taken to a primary health centre at the nearby Tissa village, where he was given first aid and then referred to Chamba hospital.
In Solan, Dilman native Seeta was returning home from her brotherâs house in Mohar village along with her two children when a bear attacked her in a forested area. As Seeta fought back, her children cried for help. Hearing them, passersby rushed to the spot and the bear fled. tnn However, by the time Seeta was rescued, she had received serious injuries. The bear had pulled the skin from her scalp and also hurt her arms.
Sources said on seeing her serious condition, people took her to Solan hospital in an ambulance where doctors provided her treatment. Her condition is said to be out of danger.
In Himachal Pradesh, attacks by wild animals, especially bear and leopard, rise during winter. Most recently, a man was mauled to death by a bear in a village in Kullu district on October 27. 
Reportedly, a bear had attacked three villagers who were out for irrigation work at one of the âkuhls.â While two managed to escape despite injuries, the third succumbed to deep injuries inflicted on his neck and genitals.

headline: Leopard kills Uttarakhand boy, state’s 9th animal conflict death this year - The Times of India
summary: A boy was killed by a leopard in Uttarakhand.
article_body:
DEHRADUN: A leopard attack claimed the life of yet another child in Dehradun marking the ninth human fatality in less than two months in human-wildlife conflict across the state. Riasat Ali, 9, was attacked by the animal while he was outside his home in the Madari Van Gujjar Basti area at Kimadi on the Mussoorie-Dehradun road.
Witnesses said Riasat had stepped out of his hutment to relieve himself when the leopard ambushed him.
Despite frantic efforts from family members and friends to rescue him, the boy succumbed to his injuries. The incident reignited fears among the city residents, especially those living on the outskirts of Dehradun who have been advised to exercise caution and follow appropriate wildlife coexistence measures.
Shamli Kumari, a 52-year-old resident of Sahastradhara area, expressed grave concern about the situation. "We are refraining from venturing out after sunset, but with the change in season, many people have no choice but to go out for morning and evening walks for good health. Leopard scare shouldn't confine residents indoors. There has to be a solution for this."
Dehradun district forest officer (DFO) Nitish Mani Tripathi said that measures were being taken to address the situation. "The Madari Chuk area is surrounded by forests. We have installed five cages and 30 camera traps, along with deploying teams for trapping the leopard," he said. "In case of adverse situation, permission from the chief wildlife warden has been sought to eliminate the leopard if it is not possible to capture the animal."
This incident is the latest in a series of attacks in the region this year (see graphic). The incidents have also raised concerns about the safety of children, with forest authorities taking additional steps to safeguard vulnerable groups. In areas like Rudraprayag and Nainital districts, which have seen a number of wildlife attacks, frontline forest department staff have been deployed to protect students en route to schools.
Tthe leopard scare has gripped children immensely, in most recent incidents, in Rudraprayag's Mahargaon Kartik Singh (15) was attacked by a leopard on Feb 20.

headline: 17-year-old mauled by leopard in Uttarakhand's Tehri - The Times of India

NEW TEHRI: A 17-year-old boy has been mauled by a leopard in Uttarakhand's Tehri district, officials said on Friday. The incident took place in Devprayag on Thursday night when Anurag, a class 12 student, was returning home after playing cricket and was attacked by the leopard, Kirtinagar sub-divisional magistrate Sonia Pant said. 
Despite some local people raising an alarm, the leopard did not leave the boy, the officials said.

The victim's mutilated body was recovered late Thursday night, Pant said. 
BJP MLA from Devprayag Vinod Kandari, who reached the spot on Friday, directed the forest department to capture the leopard immediately. 
By 6 am, a team of the forest department successfully trapped the leopard in a cage, the officials said. 
However, the angry locals created a ruckus, demanding that the leopard be shot on the spot, they said. 
The forest department officials told them that the captured leopard would be taken only to the office in the tehsil, to which they agreed. 
Upon reaching the tehsil, when the local people discovered that the leopard was being transported to Dehradun via Hindolakhal, they threw out the employees of the ranger office and staged a sit-in, locking the place, the officials said. 
Divisional forest officer Jeevan Dagade calmed the people down and appealed to them to not let their children go out of homes alone in the evening.

headline: 36 dead in wildlife attacks till June this yr, leopards top killers - The Times of India
summary: Cumulative total of 36 deaths from wildlife attacks this year, with leopards being the top killers.
article_body:
Dehradun:
 Uttarakhand has recorded 36 human deaths in wildlife attacks during the first six months of 2026âaveraging six fatalities per monthâwith big cats accounting for the vast majority of the toll, according to recent forest department data.
Leopards were responsible for the highest number of fatalities at 15, followed closely by tigers at 11. The remaining deaths were attributed to elephants (5), crocodiles (3), and a bear and snake (1 each). With these latest casualties, the total number of human lives lost to human-wildlife conflict in Uttarakhand since its formation has reached 1,325.
Leopards also caused significant non-fatal injuries, with at least 46 people attacked by the animal in the same six-month period. For comparison, leopards claimed 18 lives and tigers claimed 12 in 2025, while 15 people were killed by leopards and 12 by tigers in 2024. Overall, 68 human lives were lost to wildlife attacks in 2025, down from 84 in 2024.
Given that tiger deaths (11) and leopard deaths (15) in just the first half of this year are already nearing previous annual figures, experts warn that total fatalities for 2026 may match or exceed last yearâs annual totals.
Wildlife experts attribute the sustained pressure from tiger attacks to habitat saturation in and around the Corbett Tiger Reserve, which is pushing younger tigers into buffer zones and village fringes in search of territory.
Meanwhile, the high number of leopard cases reflects the predatorâs extensive distribution across human-settled landscapes.
Joy Hukil, a veteran private wildlife shooter deployed during recent big cat tranquilising and elimination exercises, shared insights from his decade-long field experience. âThe overpopulation of leopards and tigers is the key reason behind these escalating cases. Conservation efforts must extend beyond policy discussions and be backed by effective, science-based management on the ground,â Hukil said.
âWe need accurate assessments of predator and prey populations, along with the availability of water, habitat and food resources across every landscape in the state. A balanced ecosystem and informed wildlife management can significantly reduce human-wildlife conflict,â Hukil said.
In response to the prevailing situation, the forest department has intensified operations in conflict hotspots. Measures currently being deployed include lemongrass plantations to deter wildlife, AI-based virtual walls, and the deployment of additional Quick Response Teams (QRTs) among others. The state has also announced the opening of rescue centers across all 13 districts, apart from special incentives to boost community awareness and engage locals in promoting human-wildlife coexistence.

headline: Villagers in Uttarakhand hold forest officials hostage after series of leopard attacks on livestock - The New Indian Express
summary: Villagers in Uttarakhand held forest officials hostage following multiple leopard attacks on livestock.
article_body:
DEHRADUN: In a dramatic turn of events, villagers in Mehalchouri and Kunigad areas of Gairsain in Chamoli district, Uttarakhand, took forest officials hostage for over two hours on Thursday night.
The villagers' patience snapped after a leopard killed a cow and its calf in the Ujetiya village, bringing the total number of livestock killed in the past one month to several. The villagers had been demanding the installation of a cage to capture the leopard, which has been on a rampage, attacking livestock in the area.
The latest incident sparked outrage among the villagers, who detained forest officials, demanding immediate action to capture the big cat. The villagers released the officials after a two-hour standoff, but not before warning of further agitation if their demands are not met.
"We have reached our breaking point," said a resident, requesting anonymity. "If the leopard is targeting our cattle so openly, how long before it turns its attention to our children and the elderly?"
The affected zone lies near the sensitive border between the Garhwal and Kumaon regions. This single leopard, or possibly more, has caused widespread tension in the areas.
In Bhandarikod (Garhwal side), the predator reportedly killed three cows belonging to Krishna Nand Thapliyal. Earlier the same day, an attack was reported on Mohan Singh’s pet dog in Ujetiya, leaving it injured.
The carnage extends across the administrative boundary into Almora district (Kumaon side). Villagers in Pasara Gaon, Purana-lohba, and Nawan have reported five more cattle kills attributed to the leopard.
Driven by desperation, the enraged villagers of Ujetiya detained the on-site forest staff to demand immediate action. The standoff was resolved only after District Panchayat Member Suresh Bisht arrived and assured the community that traps would be installed immediately. Following the release of the officials, the villagers proceeded to bury the remains of the slain animals after post-mortem formalities.
Bisht, expressing grave concern, suggested the leopard might be turning man-eater due to the severity and frequency of the attacks. "I have been in discussions with the DFO at the district headquarters," Bisht confirmed. "Following talks with the Conservator, permission has now been granted to set up cages in the affected area."
Local leaders, including Gram Pradhan Deepa Devi of Silanga and Block Panchayat Member Virendra Negi, demanded swift action, citing rapid success in Almora where traps were placed just two days after incidents there.
Divisional Forest Officer Pradeep Gaur confirmed the installation of cages and an increase in forest patrol frequency. "We have deployed the necessary equipment and increased vigilance," Gaur stated, appealing to the public to remain cautious.
Meanwhile, sources within the Forest Department revealed that Uttarakhand lost 12 people to leopard attacks and seven to tiger attacks in 2024.

headline: Uttarakhand: Leopard kills elderly in Almora village - The Times of India
summary: An elderly person was killed by a leopard in Almora, Uttarakhand.
article_body:
ALMORA: A 62-year-old man was killed by a leopard on Tuesday night in Udal village of Bhaisiachhana block in Almora. The man was identified as Ramesh Ram. The leopard attacked him when he was returning home from Petsal market, situated some distance away from his village. 
Forest department officials confirmed the killing by big cat and have informed that they recovered the mutilated body of the deceased.
"When the deceased did not return home, his family members began to search for him. In the morning, his mutilated body was found in a nearby forest. We have sent the body for postmortem examination," Sanchita Verma, Almora (Badechina division) range officer, told TOI. The official added that the victimâs kin have been given an immediate aid of Rs 50,000. âThe remaining amount of compensation will be given to them after the autopsy report comes in," she added. 
Following the killing, residents demanded the forest department to declare the leopard a man-eater. Verma said that the department has written to chief wildlife warden regarding the killing and has asked for permission to set up cages to catch the leopard. She said that after the postmortem report comes, senior officials of the department will decide whether or not to declare the leopard a man-eater.

headline: Leopard attacks trigger fear, anger in Uttarakhand’s Pauri Garhwal; forest officials intensify Ops - The Shillong Times
summary: Leopard attacks are causing fear and anger, leading to intensified operations.
article_body:
Pauri Garhwal, May 2: An atmosphere of fear and anger continues to grip parts of Uttarakhand’s Pauri Garhwal district as repeated incidents of leopard attacks have left residents deeply distressed, prompting the Forest Department to intensify measures aimed at curbing human-animal conflict. The situation worsened after a fatal attack on April 24, when a 62-year-old woman, Sita Khanduri, was killed in Bamthi village under the Pauri block.
The incident marked the fifth death caused by a leopard in the area and has led to growing resentment among villagers. Officials said this is the 23rd death resulting from wildlife attacks reported in the state so far this year. According to accounts from the day of the incident, the victim was carrying out routine household work near her home when a leopard, reportedly lying in wait, suddenly attacked and killed her.
Since then, fear has spread across the village, with residents hesitant to step out of their homes. In response, the Forest Department has stepped up its operations. Providing an update, Garhwal Divisional Forest Officer Mahitam Yadav said teams are actively patrolling the affected areas around the clock.
“Surveillance has been significantly intensified during the evening hours to closely monitor the leopard’s movements. Five cages have been deployed in the affected zone; additionally, trap cameras and solar-powered cameras have been installed to track the leopard’s exact location,” Yadav told IANS.
He added that clear instructions have been issued by higher authorities regarding handling the situation. The primary aim is to capture the leopard at the earliest, followed by efforts to control it if needed, while elimination has been kept as a last resort. Mahitam Yadav said the entire Forest Department team is working continuously and making all possible efforts to capture the animal as soon as possible.
Residents in the area have also been advised to remain alert, while the department has assured all necessary support to the local population. However, villagers have alleged that despite repeated incidents in the past, adequate preventive action was not taken in time, allowing the situation to escalate. They have demanded immediate steps to capture the leopard and restore a sense of safety in the region.
The incident is part of a wider pattern of human-wildlife conflict in Uttarakhand. On April 22, a woman was killed in a similar leopard attack in Nainital. Earlier, on April 11, villagers in Balmara in Pauri Garhwal district locked over 15 officials from the block administration and Forest Department inside a panchayat office during a meeting convened to address the threat posed by a man-eating leopard that had already claimed two lives within a week.
The most recent victim at that time was 45-year-old Prakash Lal, who was attacked and killed while returning home from work. The agitated villagers later released the officials after they were assured that the leopard would be captured or eliminated within a few days. Government data indicates that wild animals, including leopards and bears, have killed more than 100 people in the state over the past five years.
However, locals claim the actual number is much higher, attributing the rise in attacks to increased human intrusion into forest areas due to road expansion and development activities. Acknowledging the seriousness of the situation, Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami earlier this month announced an increase in compensation for families of victims killed in wildlife attacks, raising it from Rs 6 lakh to Rs 10 lakh.
He also set aside Rs 5 crore for a dedicated programme aimed at rescuing wild animals that stray into human settlements, along with an additional allocation of Rs 131 crore to develop a comprehensive mechanism to address and reduce incidents of human-animal conflict in the state.
IANS

headline: Woman killed, another injured in bear attack in Chamba’s Kalwara forest - The Tribune
summary: A woman was killed and another injured in a bear attack in Chamba.
article_body:
Woman killed, another injured in bear attack in Chamba’s Kalwara forest
The victims were collecting fodder for their cattle in the Kalwara forest near their village when the bears attacked them
A woman was mauled to death and another seriously injured after being attacked by bears in the Dhimla panchayat in Chamba on Friday. The victims, Pinki Devi (44) and her sister-in-law Thanthi Devi (56), were collecting fodder for their cattle in the Kalwara forest near their village when the bears attacked them.
Pinki Devi succumbed to her injuries, while Thanthi Devi, who sustained serious injuries, has been admitted to Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru Government Medical College, where her condition is stated to be stable. According to Pawan Kumar, the deceased’s nephew, the incident occurred around 10 am. Villagers rushed to the scene after hearing their screams and managed to scare the bears away. They then rushed the victims to a nearby health facility, where Pinki Devi was pronounced dead on arrival.
A team of forest department officials arrived at the scene and are taking measures to drive the bears back into the forest, including bursting firecrackers and making loud noises with drums. Chamba Chief Conservator of Forests Abhilash Damodran said an immediate relief of Rs 10,000 has been provided to the family of the deceased woman and Rs 5,000 to the family of the injured. Further compensation will be provided to the family of the deceased once the case is processed.
The forests in Chamba district are home to several wild animal species, including Himalayan Black Bear and Himalayan Brown Bear. Bear sightings and encounters are common in Chamba, with black bears often venturing into habitations in search of food, resulting in encounters with humans. Several bear attacks have been reported across the district this year, highlighting the ongoing human-wildlife conflict in the region. Recently, a bear had ventured into a sweet shop in Jot village, and in another incident, a female bear and her cub were electrocuted to death after climbing an electric transformer in Dalhousie town.

headline: UP: Villagers kill sixth and final wolf ending months-long havoc by predator in Bahraich - Organiser
summary: Villagers killed a wolf after months of attacks.
article_body:
After months of terror, the six-member wolf pack responsible for wreaking havoc in the Mahsi region of Bahraich has finally been eradicated. The last wolf was beaten to death by villagers in Tamachpur village on Saturday while attempting to hunt a goat.
Following this, the forest department came to the village and recovered the body of the wolf. Further action will be taken after the postmortem of the wolf’s body.
“For many days the department’s teams were trying to catch this last wolf. When we got information that there was an animal body lying in a village. We immediately went there with our team and saw that a dead wolf was lying there since there were marks of wounds on his body. It is possible that these villagers or some other people killed it. We will investigate this. Only after investigation will we be able to say anything further,” Bahraich District Forest Officer Ajit Singh said.
For the past few months, this pack of six wolves had wreaked havoc across many villages in the Mahsi tehsil in the Bahraich district of Uttar Pradesh.
Earlier, the Uttar Pradesh Forest Department had initiated “Operation Bhediya” to apprehend the pack of wolves responsible for recent attacks in 25-30 villages under Mahsi tehsil in the Bahraich range of Bahraich Forest Division.
The Forest Department had captured the fifth ‘killer’ wolf on September 10.
In order to capture the sixth wolf, the Forest Department in Bahraich had installed snap cameras at most of the probable habitats of wolves in the area to monitor any movement.
Three snap-cameras were installed in Sikandarpur village around six caves, which local villagers claim to be the habitat of the wolves.
Nine people were killed and more than 40 people have been injured until now due to the attacks by the man-eater wolves in various villages of Bahraich.
(With inputs from ANI)

headline: Wolf attacks in UP: Man-eater wolf attacks 5-year-old girl in Bahraich - PTC News

Wolf attacks in UP: Man-eater wolf attacks 5-year-old girl in Bahraich
Wolf attacks in UP: In a fresh attack by a man-eater wolf in Uttar Pradesh's Bahraich, a five-year-old girl was injured last night in the Mahasi Tehsil area. headline: 28-year-old woman injured in attack by man-eater wolf in UP's Bahraich - India Today

article_body:
28-year-old woman injured in attack by man-eater wolf in UP's Bahraich
The animal attacked a villager for a fourth consecutive day in Bahraich since the fifth of the six wolves on the loose in the region was caught by the authorities.
A 28-year-old woman was attacked by a wolf and sustained injuries to her neck and chest in Uttar Pradesh's Bahraich, officials said on Friday.
The latest attack took place in Singiya Nasirpur village in Bahraich, which has been affected by wolf attacks for some time now.
The animal attacked a villager for a fourth consecutive day in the area since the fifth of the six wolves on the loose in the region was caught by the authorities.
Wolf attacks continue unabated as people are living in fear as the man-eater animals are on the loose in the area. The escalating threat of wild animal attacks has sparked concern among locals.Â
Meanwhile, the authorities are trying their best to catch the wolf, but hardly any strategy seems to be working as continuous heavy rain in Bahraich is hampering search operations in the affected area.Â
The Singiya Nasirpur incident came a day after two separate jackal attacks left several villagers injured, including a 10-year-old boy. A jackal was also caught on camera moving through a field, prompting the Forest Department to be on high alert.
These recent incidents come amid an ongoing crisis in Bahraich, where wolves have claimed the lives of over 10 people and injured dozens more. headline: 12 injured in jackal attack in UP's Pilibhit amid wolf terror in Bahraich - India Today
summary: 12 individuals were injured in a jackal attack in Pilibhit, Uttar Pradesh.
article_body:
12 injured in jackal attack in UP's Pilibhit amid wolf terror in Bahraich
A pack of jackals attacked people in two villages in Uttar Pradesh's Pilibhit district in which at least 12 people, including seven children, were injured.
At least 12 people, including five children, were injured after being attacked by a pack of jackals in two villages in Uttar Pradesh's Pilibhit district.
According to the locals, the jackals first attacked children in Suswar and Pansoli villages in Jahanabad area when they were playing outside their homes. When some elderly people rushed to protect the children, the wild animal also attacked them.
After the attack, all 12 people were admitted to Jahanabad's Community Health Centre (CHC), where they were receiving necessary treatment.
Enraged by the attack from the jackals, the locals then kill one of them.
Upon receiving an alert about the jackal attacks, a team from the local administration and forest department rushed to the spot and started an investigation into the incident.
The attack by jackals in Pilibhit came at a time when wolf attacks in neighbouring Bahraich district have killed a total of 10 people, including several children.
About 36 people, including women, children and the elderly have also been injured in wolf attacks in Bahraich.
Speaking about the attacks by a pack of jackals, Pilibhit's District Forest Officer (DFO) Manish Singh said some villagers earlier claimed that the attack was done by a pack of wolves but it was later confirmed that a jackal was behind it.
"We are monitoring the situation. These jackals have become aggressive because the rains have flooded their hiding places, forcing them out. Also, it is their mating period, during which they tend to be more aggressive. We are keeping a close watch on them."
Meanwhile, Pilibhit's MP Jitin Prasada also spoke to the locals about the incident over the phone.

headline: Wild boar attacks wreak havoc in Hajin, injure woman, damage rice nursery beds - Kashmir Reader
summary: Wild boar attacks in Hajin resulted in injuries to a woman and damage to rice nursery beds.
article_body:
Farmers demand immediate steps to tackle menace
BANDIPORA: A wave of fear and distress has gripped the town of Hajin in north Kashmir’s Bandipora district as wild boars continue to wreak havoc, leaving residents and farmers in a state of shock.
On Tuesday, a 65-year-old woman, Sarwa Begum, wife of Hajin resident Ghulam Hassan Wani, became the latest victim of a wild boar attack.
Eyewitnesses recounted how the boar emerged in the orchard fields and aggressively targeted the woman, leaving her injured. After receiving initial treatment at CHC Hajin, she was referred to JVC for further medical attention.
This incident comes just days after a 56-year-old man was also injured in a similar attack, underscoring the escalating threat posed by wild boars in the area.
Meanwhile, the wild boars have unleashed chaos in the Hajin, leaving residents reeling in shock.
Their latest rampage has targeted rice nursery beds, dealing a severe blow to the agricultural community in the area.
The locals said that the increasing population of wild boars in Hajin is creating problems for the farmers in the area. They said the animals destroy the crops in the fields causing heavy losses.
Farmers, who depend on these nursery beds to plant paddy crops, are facing an unprecedented challenge this year as many rice nursery beds were damaged in the area.
They said the relentless onslaught of the wild boars may render it impossible for farmers to carry out their usual agricultural practices this year due to extensive damage to the nursery beds. The damage inflicted by the boars cuts deep through the heart of the town’s agricultural sector, they said.
Sajad Ahmad, a farmer, said the wild boars are damaging crops including paddy and vegetables, besides vegetables. He said if immediate steps are not taken immediately, the losses would be very high in future.
Expressing their dismay and frustration, farmers have called upon the wildlife department and administration to intervene swiftly and effectively to address this pressing issue before further damage is done to livelihoods in the area.
They warned that failure to do so could lead to irreparable damage to the town’s agricultural sector and livelihoods of its residents.

headline: Hoshiarpur: Wild boar attack on crop leaves farmers worried - The Tribune
summary: Wild boar attacks have left farmers in Hoshiarpur worried about crop damage.
article_body:
Aakanksha N Bhardwaj
Jalandhar, June 20
In a week, paddy transplantation will start and Parminder Singh, a farmer from Dadiana Kalan from Hoshiarpur, is ready with crackers, phenyl, iron wires and a battery to keep wild boars away.
Assurance to farmers
The wild boar issue is troubling farmers a lot. Yes, the area under maize has reduced. We will definitely adopt measures so that the cultivation of maize increases. Kewal Singh, CAO
Apart from worrying about the input cost, growth of paddy and income, another major worry that has engrossed his mind is how to tackle the attack of wild boars on the crop. He is not alone, the farmers living near Kandi and Bet areas in Hoshiarpur have this fear. They burst crackers and spread phenyl clothes outside their fields so that the smell keeps off the boars.
Farmers have also installed an iron wire along the fields with a battery that creates current in the wire. “Last year, I had sown maize on 1.5 acres but wild boars ravaged my entire field and I was just left with 10 corncobs (challis). I had suffered a heavy loss. There was an input cost of Rs 40,000 in preparing the crop on 1.5 acres,” Parminder said.
The gravity of the problem is such that the farmers have started reducing area under other crops like maize, paddy, groundnuts and have switched to agroforestry.
As per the information received from the Agriculture Department, the decrease of 7,000 hectares and 5,000 hectares of area has been witnessed in the case of maize and paddy crop over the years.
Another farmer Jaswinder Singh from Lambra village said, “Whenever a boar try to enter the field and touches iron wires, it gets shocked. But, it is very costly. Not only this, we also make rounds of our fields at night with torch. I used to grow maize, paddy along with sugarcane on eight acres of fields, but now I have switched to growing of trees.”
The area under poplar and eucalyptus has increased from 15,000 hectares in 2019 to more than 25,000 hectares this time. With the mushrooming of plywood factories in the area, the switch to poplar and eucalyptus has become a great source of earning for farmers.
They have been demanding subsidy on electric fence which can be a suitable alternative to shoo away wild boars. Senior officials from the administration say that the subsidy on electric fencing, which was stopped years ago, should be restored as it will be of a great help to the farmers. “The wild boars attack on the crops is affecting farmers’ income. The permits to shoot wild boars are also issued by the SDMs after checking every detail properly,” Komal Mittal, Hoshiarpur DC.

headline: Wild boars attack UP farmer, chew his genital - The Times of India
summary: A farmer in Uttar Pradesh suffered injury due to an attack by wild boars.
article_body:
SHAHJAHANPUR: In a bizarre incident, a group of wild boars attacked a couple of farmers in Shahjahanpurâs Lalpur area on Wednesday night and chewed the private parts of one of them while injuring the other.
 The victim, Ram Manohar, 55, had gone to answer natureâs call in a sugarcane field when a fully-grown adult wild boar suddenly emerged from bushes and attacked him.
 Local residents rushed to him after hearing his shrieks and rescued him as they drove the animal away with sticks. 
 Manohar, parts of whose thigh and private parts were chewed by the boar, was taken to the local community health centre from where he was referred to the district hospital.
 In the meanwhile, the group of wild boars rushed out of the cane field and injured another villager, identified as Ram Sahay, who was sitting outside his house.
 Panic gripped the area where villagers kept vigil throughout the night with stick and torches.
 Dr 
Sandeep Verma
, superintendent of health centre, said, âThe injuries on the victimâs private parts were serious. Hence, we referred him to the district hospital.â
 Balhar Singh, a local farmer, told TOI, âWild boars are a huge menace for us as they are fond of sugarcane and often destroy our entire crop. It is extremely difficult to take them out of the field if they come in a herd. There are no carnivores in the adjacent forest area and this is why their population is increasing day by day.â
 Divisional forest officer Manoj Khare said, âIt is an unfortunate incident, but there is nothing much we can do to control wild boars and nilgais. We can provide permission to shoot wild boars if someone asks for it; however, there is no provision of providing any compensation to the victim by forest department.â
 Boar attacks on humans have been documented since the Stone Age, with one of the oldest depictions being a cave painting in Bhimbetaka in Madhya Pradesh. 
 A 2012 study compiling recorded attacks from 1825â2012 found accounts of 665 human victims of both wild boars and feral pigs, with the majority (19%) of attacks in the animalâs native range occurring in India. Attacks on humans are rare, but can be serious, resulting in multiple penetrating injuries to the lower part of the body. The animal typically attacks by charging and pointing its tusks towards the intended victim, with most injuries occurring on the thigh region.
